hints: Look at the shape of the given $v$ against $t$ graph: a straight line through the origin.
Recall that the gradient of a $v$-$t$ graph equals $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$.
Ask what happens to $v$ while that gradient stays the same, then picture that on axes of $v$ vertical against $a$ horizontal.
walkthrough: The given graph is $v$ against $t$ starting at $0$ and rising with a constant straight-line gradient.
Use $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$ = gradient of $v$-$t$ graph, so a constant gradient means $a$ has one constant positive value throughout.
Meanwhile $v$ starts at zero and keeps increasing with $t$.
On the new axes, $a$ is horizontal and $v$ is vertical, so a fixed $a$ is one horizontal position.
Increasing $v$ at that fixed $a$ is a vertical line rising from near the $a$-axis.

options.A: This shows $v$ changing as $a$ changes, but $a$ does not change in this motion.
options.B: This shows $v$ increasing as $a$ increases, but the $v$-$t$ gradient and so $a$ is fixed.
options.C: This shows $v$ fixed while $a$ varies, which reverses what happens: $a$ is fixed while $v$ increases.
options.D: Acceleration is constant from the straight $v$-$t$ graph, so $v$ increases vertically at one value of $a$.
